title: Turn a cake out onto a plate: clamp plate and pan together with both hands, turn them over and lift the pan off
instruction: Turn the cake out of its pan onto the plate without damaging it, so that it ends up upside down on the plate on the stand with the pan off it.
context: Turning a freshly baked cake out of its tin is a step in nearly every home cake recipe, familiar to anyone who bakes at home, and it is done the same way in home kitchens and bakeries: a plate (or rack) goes upside down on the tin, both hands hold plate and tin together from opposite sides, and the two are turned over as one so the cake drops onto the plate; then the tin is lifted off (recipe writers describe the same hold-both-and-flip move, e.g. Alice Medrich's Food52 column on getting cakes out of their pans). Held from one side only, the stack hangs off that grip and comes apart, and the plate is far wider than one hand. A sponge cake is soft: squeezed it dents and dropped or bent it cracks, so the hands hold the plate and the tin, never the cake. The instruction states only the result.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. A fixed pale blue cake stand (a pedestal 13 cm across and 10 cm tall with a non-slip silicone top) stands 30 cm forward on the centre line. On it sits a round anodised-aluminium cake pan (about 1.9 mm sheet, 200 g): 14 cm across and 3.6 cm deep inside, with an ordinary narrow flat rim 7 mm wide around its top (16 cm across) and two flat tab handles riveted to the rim, 3 cm wide, reaching 13 cm from its centre towards each arm. In the middle of the pan lies a plain sponge cake, crust up: a disc 12.7 cm across and 2.8 cm tall (about 100 g) cut with a 12.7 cm (5-inch) round cutter from a store-bought, un-iced, unfilled round sponge cake layer (for example Rich's Allen un-iced round sponge cake, 7-8 inch, 11.22 oz, sold frozen in cases of 24) and levelled to 2.8 cm, at room temperature (20-25 °C). A flat white ABS plastic plate, 21 cm across and 6 mm thick (220 g), lies on the pan's rim and handles, covering the pan. The pan, the cake and the plate are loose. Friction in the simulation (static / dynamic): pan and plate 0.6 / 0.5, cake 0.7 / 0.6, the stand's silicone top and the gripper pads 1.2 / 1.0. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged from the overhead and wrist videos and, after the run, with a steel ruler and a photo. Damaged cake: 0, whatever else happened, if after the run the cake's height, measured with the ruler upright against its side at four points (front, back, left, right), is under 2.5 cm at any of them (it was cut to 2.8 cm: squashed by more than 3 mm), a ruler laid across it shows a dent 3 mm or deeper, or a photo from above with the ruler beside it shows a crack longer than 2 cm or a piece larger than 1 cm broken off. (The simulation's scorer latches 0 for the rest of the run once an arm presses on the cake with more than 3 N, its two halves are squashed together by more than 3 mm, or they break apart.) Otherwise the best stage reached during the run: 0.25: the cake has lain upside down (crust down, turned more than 160 degrees) on the plate, its middle within 2.5 cm of the plate's, touching it (within 3 mm). 0.5: it lies like that on the plate with the plate flat on the stand (within 10 degrees of level, its middle within 3 cm of the stand's, resting on it within 3 mm), all still. 1.0: that, with the pan lifted off and away (its middle 15 cm or more from the cake's), both grippers released and 4 cm or more from the cake and the plate, the cake undamaged and everything still for 2 s.
reset_notes: Cakes: keep the sponge layers frozen (-18 °C or colder) until the day of the trials and thaw one in its wrapping at room temperature (20-25 °C) before cutting. Preparing a cake takes about 3 minutes: cut a disc with a 12.7 cm round cutter, level it to 2.8 cm with a serrated knife run along two 2.8 cm guide sticks (the browned top stays as its crust) and weigh it (use discs within 10 g of the first one used). Keep cut cakes covered at room temperature, use them the same day and handle them with food-safe gloves; they are dry (no icing, filling or syrup) and leave only crumbs. Reset (about 1 minute): brush crumbs off the pan, the plate and the grippers; if the cake passed the damage check, slide it back into the middle of the pan crust up on a flat spatula, otherwise use a fresh disc; put the pan on the stand and the plate on its rim.
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.1, 20 Hz control). The sponge cake is two rigid halves on a sprung slide joint (6,000 N/m) that breaks under 40 N or 0.3 N m: an arm pressing on it with more than 3 N (enough to dent sponge), the halves squashed more than 3 mm, or the joint broken stand in for the dents and cracks the simulator cannot show; no sticking to the pan. The pan is one rigid body (floor, 24 wall and 24 rim panels, two handles). Friction per material: pan, plate 0.6; cake 0.7; silicone 1.2.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both grippers went to the stack's sides and reached for the plate's edge and the pan's handles several times, nudging the plate on the pan, but never clamped and turned the stack; the cake stayed in the pan); demo: 1.0
